narrative.h2: Worship video is its own genre with its own canon

sections.heading: What worship video actually looks like
sections.body: The visual canon is well-defined: Hillsong, Elevation, Bethel, Maverick City — lyric-forward typography over a live congregation shot in warm tungsten, slow camera moves, the worship leader rarely the dominant frame. The lyrics matter because the audience is meant to sing along, so on-screen text is non-negotiable and the type design is closer to publishing than to pop-video kineticism. The aesthetic is intimate live performance, not produced pop video.

sections.heading: Shots and conventions that work
sections.body: Wide of the congregation with hands raised, soft-focus, warm key from the stage lights. Medium of the worship leader, eyes closed, mid-phrase. Insert of a single congregant during the bridge — usually older, usually emotional, intentionally not the prettiest face in the room. Lyric text appears line-by-line, centered, in a clean serif or humanist sans, with enough lead-in time for the congregation to read before they sing. Cuts land on phrase ends, not on the beat.

sections.heading: How Tunee handles the worship preset
sections.body: The Worship preset goes lyric-forward by default — every line of the song appears on screen with the line-by-line reveal timing the format requires. The visual base layer skews toward warm-lit congregational shots and softly-lit instrumentalist frames, with optional uploads of your actual church's footage to ground the generated material in your community. Output is 16:9 for in-service projection plus 9:16 for the social cuts that drive Sunday attendance during the week.
